proof_text:
Existence follows directly from the construction of
$\mathbb{C} = \mathbb{R} \oplus i\mathbb{R}$, where
$x = \operatorname{Re}(z)$ and $y = \operatorname{Im}(z)$.

To establish uniqueness, suppose that $z = x_1 + i y_1 = x_2 + i y_2$
for real numbers $x_1, x_2, y_1, y_2 \in \mathbb{R}$. Rearranging this
equality in the field $\mathbb{C}$ yields:
$$ (x_1 - x_2) = i(y_2 - y_1). $$ Squaring both sides and using
$i^2 = -1$, we obtain:
$$ (x_1 - x_2)^2 = i^2 (y_2 - y_1)^2 = -(y_2 - y_1)^2. $$ Since
$x_1 - x_2$ and $y_2 - y_1$ are real numbers, their squares are
non-negative: $(x_1 - x_2)^2 \ge 0$ and $-(y_2 - y_1)^2 \le 0$. The
only real number that is simultaneously non-negative and non-positive
is zero. Therefore: $$ (x_1 - x_2)^2 = 0 \implies x_1 = x_2, $$ and
$$ -(y_2 - y_1)^2 = 0 \implies y_1 = y_2. $$ Thus the real and
imaginary parts are uniquely determined.

Theorem:
given: z is \complex
then:
. existsUnique: x is \real
  suchThat:
  . existsUnique: y is \real
    suchThat: z = x \.complex.+./ (y \.complex.*./ \complex.i)
Documented:
. called: "Uniqueness of Cartesian Form"
. description: "Every complex number has a unique representation $x+iy$ with
                real coordinates $x$ and $y$."
